terms.grammar: impersonal: habet stands for rēs sē habet, “the thing holds well”
evidence: Cic. Mur. 14: bene habet: jacta sunt fundāmenta dēfēnsiōnis (Lewis & Short), s.v. bene
Hor. S. 2.6.4: bene est. nīl amplius ōrō
Cic. Att. 1.7: apud mātrem rēctē est, she is quite well (Lewis & Short), s.v. regō
terms.comment: Of people, it says they are well: apud mātrem rēctē est, all is well at your mother’s.

evidence: Traupman 18: everything is O.K., omnia sunt pulchrē
terms.comment: Latin uses an adverb with esse where English has an adjective, as in pulchrē est mihi, I am well (Cic. N. D. 1.114, Lewis & Short); the phrase with omnia is Traupman’s. He also gives omnia sunt fēlīciter and omnia sunt fēstīviter, which Lewis & Short does not support: fēstīviter is ante- and post-classical, “merrily”.

evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. probus: “in responses, as a token of applause”

phrases.english: it is good. I ask for nothing more
